claims.text: An active-learning machine-learned free-energy integration framework with sparse ab initio molecular-dynamics corrections will substantially reduce computational cost in multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The proposed framework will maintain the fidelity of fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The target systems are multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their fusion points, with both solid and liquid phases represented.
Full explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations can be replaced by a surrogate machine-learned interatomic potential with periodic sparse, targeted ab initio sampling.
Umbrella sampling or thermodynamic integration can be used to target the sparse ab initio corrections.
The method is applicable within approximately ±10% of the fusion temperature.
Near-equimolar compositions are typical of high-entropy alloys.
Active refinement of the machine-learned potential-energy surface in critical regions will capture vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling effects.
The machine-learned surrogate will rapidly sample much larger regions of phase space than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Sparse ab initio corrections will preserve the entropy contributions needed for accurate solid and liquid free energies.
The approach will drastically reduce the number of computationally intensive ab initio molecular-dynamics simulations required.
The method will provide orders-of-magnitude speed improvement over explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
The method will significantly outperform TOR-TILD in throughput for multicomponent systems.
Predicted phase free energies, melting temperatures, and latent heats will remain within a small error margin of full ab initio molecular-dynamics benchmarks.
Reliability will be greatest in composition regions sufficiently covered by sparse ab initio corrections.
The hypothesis is falsified if computational cost is not reduced by at least one order of magnitude relative to the traditional workflow.
